items.q: Two Sum — find indices of two numbers adding to a target
items.prompt:
Given an `IntArray` and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target. Exactly one solution exists and you may not use the same element twice.

This is almost always the warm-up. The interviewer is checking that you go from brute force to the hash-map insight quickly, and that you state complexity without being asked.
hints: Brute force is two nested loops, O(n²). What information are you recomputing?
For each element `x`, you're looking for `target - x`. What data structure answers 'have I seen this value?' in O(1)?
Store value → index as you go, and check for the complement **before** inserting the current element so you never reuse it.

code.caption: Single pass, O(n) time / O(n) space

items.complexity: Time O(n), space O(n). The brute force is O(n²) time / O(1) space — mention the trade-off explicitly.
followUps: What if the array is sorted? (Two pointers, O(1) extra space.)
What if there are multiple valid answers and you must return all unique pairs?
Three Sum — how does the approach generalize, and why does sorting help there?

items.prompt:
Given a string, return the length of the longest substring with no repeated characters.

The canonical sliding-window problem. If you can derive the window-shrink invariant out loud, you'll pass most window questions.
hints: A substring is a contiguous range — that suggests a window with two pointers rather than generating substrings.
Expand `right` one character at a time. When does the window become invalid?
When you see a duplicate, move `left` to just past the previous occurrence of that character. Track last-seen index per character so the jump is O(1) rather than shrinking one step at a time.

code.caption: Window with last-seen index — O(n)

items.complexity: Time O(n) — each index is visited once by `right` and `left` never moves backward. Space O(min(n, alphabet)).
followUps: Longest substring with at most K distinct characters — how does the invariant change?
Minimum window substring — why does that one need a counter map rather than a set?
Why is `if (prev >= left)` necessary? What breaks without it?

items.q: Design an LRU cache with O(1) get and put
items.prompt:
Implement an LRU (least-recently-used) cache supporting `get(key)` and `put(key, value)` in O(1) average time, evicting the least recently used entry when capacity is exceeded.

**Why this one matters for Android:** it is exactly what `LruCache` and every image loader's memory cache does. Expect the follow-up "now make it thread-safe" or "now add a disk tier".
hints: You need two things at once: O(1) key lookup, and O(1) reordering of recency. One data structure gives you each.
HashMap gives lookup. A doubly-linked list gives O(1) move-to-front and O(1) removal from the tail — provided the map stores the *node*, not the value.
In Kotlin you can also get this free: `LinkedHashMap(capacity, 0.75f, accessOrder = true)` and override `removeEldestEntry`. Show you know both — implement the manual one, then mention the shortcut.

code.caption: Manual implementation — HashMap + doubly-linked list
The shortcut worth naming after you've shown the manual version

items.complexity: get / put both O(1) average. Space O(capacity). Every operation is a constant number of pointer updates plus one hash operation.
followUps: Make it thread-safe — where exactly do you synchronize, and what does that cost under contention?
Add a size-aware eviction policy (bytes, not entries) like a bitmap cache needs.
Add a disk tier: what changes about eviction and about `get` latency?
How would you implement LFU instead, and why is it harder to keep O(1)?

items.q: Implement debounced search-as-you-type that cancels stale requests
items.prompt:
Build the data path for a search screen: the user types, and you must issue a network search — but only after typing settles, never for the same query twice in a row, and a slower earlier request must never overwrite a newer result.

This is the single most common "write some Android code" exercise in a modern loop, because it tests coroutines, Flow operator choice, and race-condition awareness in one small problem.
hints: Which operator waits for a pause in emissions? Which one drops consecutive duplicates?
The stale-response race is the real question. Which flatMap variant *cancels* the in-flight inner flow when a new value arrives?
Think about where errors are caught — `catch` only sees upstream. Where must it go so a failed search doesn't kill the whole flow for the rest of the session?

code.caption: The full pipeline, with the race and the error path handled

items.complexity: No asymptotic complexity to quote — the interviewer is scoring operator choice and race handling. Say out loud: `flatMapLatest` guarantees at most one in-flight request and cancels stale ones, so out-of-order responses are impossible by construction.
followUps: Why `flatMapLatest` and not `flatMapMerge`? What bug does merge produce?
Where must `catch` go, and what happens if you put it after `stateIn`?
How would you add a local-cache-first tier so results appear instantly offline?
How would you test this deterministically? (Virtual time + `runTest` + Turbine.)

items.prompt:
Return the node values level by level, as a list of lists.

The base case for every "process a tree in layers" question — right-side view, zigzag order, level averages, and minimum depth are all one small edit away.
hints: Depth-first recursion visits nodes in the wrong order for this. What structure processes nodes in the order they were discovered?
Use a queue. But a plain BFS loses level boundaries — how do you know where one level ends?
Capture `queue.size` at the top of each iteration: that count is exactly the number of nodes in the current level.

code.caption: BFS with an explicit level-size snapshot

items.complexity: Time O(n) — every node enqueued and dequeued once. Space O(w) where w is the maximum width, which is O(n) in the worst case (a complete tree's last level).
followUps: Zigzag level order — what's the minimal change? (Reverse alternate levels, or use a deque.)
Right-side view — which element of each level do you keep?
Why is the space complexity O(w) and not O(h)?
Could you do level order with DFS? (Yes — pass depth down and index into the result list.)

items.q: House Robber — max sum with no two adjacent elements
items.prompt:
Given an array of non-negative integers, choose a subset with maximum sum such that no two chosen elements are adjacent.

The cleanest introduction to DP state design. If you can articulate the recurrence and then compress the space, you've demonstrated the whole DP toolkit in three minutes.
hints: At each index you have exactly two choices. What are they, and what does each imply about the previous index?
Define `dp[i]` = best total using the first `i` houses. Write the recurrence in terms of `dp[i-1]` and `dp[i-2]`.
`dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i])`. Now notice you only ever read two cells back — you don't need the array at all.

code.caption: O(1) space after recognizing the two-cell window
The explicit table version — write this first if it helps you think

items.complexity: Time O(n), space O(1) for the rolling version (O(n) for the table). Always mention that you'd write the table first and compress second — interviewers like seeing the derivation.
followUps: House Robber II — the houses form a circle. How does that change the problem? (Run it twice, excluding first or last.)
What if you could take at most K non-adjacent houses?
Reconstruct which houses were chosen, not just the total. What extra bookkeeping is needed?
